summary: Defines the procedures and extensions to CR-LDP needed to support unnumbered links in MPLS traffic engineering. Existing signaling did not cover links without their own IP addresses, and this document supplies the missing support.

eli5.summary: Like the matching note for another signaling system, this shows how to set up paths over links that have no address of their own, using CR-LDP.

questions: what is a forwarding adjacency in mpls
how does cr-ldp signal unnumbered links
subtitle: How CR-LDP signalling can name and use MPLS traffic engineering links that have no IP address.

tldr.problem: MPLS traffic engineering signalling had no way to indicate an unnumbered link, one without an IP address, in an Explicit Route.
tldr.mechanism: Each end of a link assigns it a 32-bit identifier, and two new TLVs carry those identifiers: one in explicit routes and one for forwarding adjacencies.
tldr.outcome: CR-LDP can set up label switched paths over unnumbered links, with the matching IGP support covered elsewhere.

today: RFC 3480 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Unnumbered Link Problem
sections.content:
Supporting MPLS traffic engineering over unnumbered links (links without IP addresses) takes two parts: carrying their traffic engineering information in the IGP (IS-IS or OSPF), and being able to specify them in signalling. This RFC covers only the signalling part, for CR-LDP; the IGP part is in other documents.

Existing signalling could not indicate an unnumbered link in its Explicit Route objects. The RFC proposes procedures and extensions to fix that.
sections.eli5: A route plan could only name roads that have addresses. This note lets it name roads without one.

sections.title: Link Identifiers and Router IDs
sections.content:
An unnumbered link has to be point-to-point. The LSR at each end assigns it an identifier: a non-zero 32-bit number unique within that LSR. There is no relationship between the two numbers. From one LSR's view its own number is the local identifier and the other's is the remote identifier.

The two ends exchange identifiers by configuration, by LMP, by CR-LDP (especially for a Forwarding Adjacency), or by IS-IS or OSPF extensions. If an IGP is used, its modules and CR-LDP must agree on the identifiers.

The Router ID is a stable IP address of an LSR that is reachable whenever the LSR is, typically a loopback address. With OSPF or IS-IS it is RECOMMENDED to be the OSPF Router Address or the IS-IS Traffic Engineering Router ID. All of this also applies to unnumbered component links of bundled links.
sections.eli5: Each end of the road picks its own number for it. The two ends tell each other their numbers so both can talk about the same road.

sections.title: Unnumbered Forwarding Adjacencies
sections.content:
When an LSR advertises a label switched path as an unnumbered Forwarding Adjacency in IS-IS or OSPF, or uses it as an unnumbered component link of a bundled link, it MUST allocate an identifier to it like any other unnumbered link. The REQUEST message that sets up the path MUST then carry an LSP_TUNNEL_INTERFACE_ID TLV with the head end's Router ID and that identifier.

If the REQUEST has that TLV, the tail-end LSR MUST allocate an identifier too, and its MAPPING message MUST carry the TLV with the tail end's Router ID and identifier. The TLV in a REQUEST is called the Forward Interface ID and in a MAPPING the Reverse Interface ID.

The head end uses its own allocation as the local identifier and the Reverse Interface ID as the remote identifier. The tail end does the opposite, using the Forward Interface ID as its remote identifier.
sections.eli5: When a whole tunnel is treated like a road, both ends of the tunnel pick a number for it and swap them in the setup messages.

sections.title: The Two New TLVs
sections.content:
The LSP_TUNNEL_INTERFACE_ID TLV has Type 0x0836 and length 8. After the type and length it holds the LSR's Router ID and a 32-bit Interface ID. It can optionally appear in a REQUEST or MAPPING message.

The Unnumbered Interface ID is a new ER-Hop type for the Explicit Route TLV. Its Type is 0x0837 and its Length is 12. The L bit is set for a loose hop and cleared for a strict hop. It holds the Router ID and the Interface ID, the identifier that the LSR named by the Router ID gave to the link.
sections.eli5: The two new labels are like address cards with two lines: whose road it is, and what number that owner gave the road.

sections.title: Processing Rules
sections.content:
When an LSR gets a REQUEST with an IF_ID TLV containing an IF_INDEX TLV, it looks for a link whose tuple of Router ID and local identifier matches the IP Address and Interface ID in the IF_INDEX TLV. A match identifies the link for label allocation. Otherwise the LSR SHOULD return an error.

An Unnumbered Interface ID ER-Hop belongs to an abstract node if the node has the same Router ID and has an unnumbered link or Forwarding Adjacency whose local identifier equals the Interface ID. Explicit Route processing then follows section 4.8.1 of RFC 3212.

When choosing the next hop, if the outgoing link is unnumbered, the REQUEST sent on MUST include the IF_ID TLV, with the IP address set to the node's Router ID and the Interface ID set to the identifier the node assigned to the link.
sections.eli5: Each router checks the road number on the route plan against its own list. If it finds a match, it knows which road to use. If not, it should complain.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC says it raises no new security issues. CR-LDP inherits the mechanism in section 4.0 of RFC 3036 that protects against spoofed TCP segments in LDP session connections.

For IANA, the CR-LDP TLV range 0x0800 to 0x08FF and its assignment rules, set in RFC 3212, apply to the two new TLV types. The RFC does not create a new registry.
sections.eli5: Nothing new needs guarding, since the usual protection for these sessions already applies.

fields.name: L
fields.desc: Set for a loose hop, cleared for a strict hop.

fields.name: Router ID
fields.desc: Router ID of the LSR that assigned the identifier.

fields.name: Interface ID
fields.desc: Identifier the LSR gave to the link.
